# Repository Guidelines

## Read This First

- This file is generated by `template agent generate` from two distinct checkouts. The command materializes the branch-tracked `[guidance.source]` declared in `<consumer-repo>/template.config.toml`, then reads reusable fragments beneath `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/**`. It reads maintainer overlays only from `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**`.
- Target filename directories inside the materialized guidance-source repository choose reusable outputs: `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/AGENTS.md/*.md` contributes root guidance, `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/crates/AGENTS.md/*.md` contributes members-directory guidance, and `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/stask/AGENTS.md/*.md` contributes local-extension guidance. A consuming repository is not expected to contain a reusable `fragments/` directory.
- Reusable files inside `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/<target-file>/**` use `<order>-<name>.md`. Target-local files inside `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/<target-file>/**` use `o<order>-<name>.md` for the dynamic tail or `s<slot>-o<order>-<name>.md` for explicit insertion after a reusable slot.
- Author target-local overlays against the composed output. Do not repeat reusable policy, ecosystem ownership, workflow rules, or cross-repository architecture in `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**`.
- Edit the owning input in either `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/**` or `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**`, then regenerate in the consumer. Never hand-edit generated `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, nested generated Markdown, or their `CLAUDE.md` companions.
- Standard `just` recipes are thin dispatchers to the installed `template` executable. Only repository-specific `just x <name>` extensions compile the local guarded `stask`.
- Lint, panic-free, coverage, mutation, generated-output, and ownership rules are design constraints. Do not weaken them or invent coverage-only scaffolding to clear a gate.

## Repository Mode and Ownership

This repository is a Rust workspace rooted at `Cargo.toml` and a consumer of the branch declared by `[template.source]` in the exact repository-root file `template.config.toml`. Workspace member placement comes from `[ecosystems.cargo.layout]`; the template default is `crates/<name>/`. CI is defined in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, while shared policy files include `clippy.toml`, `rustfmt.toml`, `deny.toml`, `dupes.toml`, and `rust-toolchain.toml`.

- **Template-maintainer mode:** when a task explicitly changes shared template policy, installed automation, generated-document machinery, or managed artifacts, work in the owning `template-rs`, `rust-template`, or `agents-md-rs` repository rather than forking the behavior locally.
- **Product-repository mode:** otherwise, the repository's workspace crates and product content are the deliverables. Treat template machinery as support and use declared deviations or repository-specific extensions for genuine local differences.
- **Single policy authority:** template, ecosystem, guidance, contract, gate, managed-child, plugin, and deviation declarations live in `template.config.toml`; do not recreate legacy Cargo metadata or Git-config keys as parallel authority.
- **Generated outputs:** coverage reports and metrics live under `cov/`; badges live under `badges/`; snapshots and compile diagnostics live beside the tests that own them.
- **Dependencies:** declare external dependencies once in root `[workspace.dependencies]`, then opt member crates into them with `.workspace = true`.

## Visibility and Reachability Are Contracts

- Treat an apparently unused item as an ownership question first. Check crate façades, downstream crates, installed command registration, extension registries, generated providers, tests, examples, fragment guidance, and known external consumers before changing visibility or deleting it.
- Local source reachability alone is not enough to retire a deliberate public API, but `pub` is not a permanent exemption from dead-code review. Every exported item must have a verified consumer contract, supported extension seam, or documented integration role.
- Remove definite reset residue once its replacement and consumers are established. Do not leave obsolete aliases, re-export preludes, disconnected modules, mirrored standard commands, or stale error variants behind after a refactor.
- When public documentation links an internal item, resolve the underlying ownership boundary: make a genuine consumer contract public with all signature types, or keep the implementation private and document the public façade.
- Verify visibility changes with the full documentation and lint gates when command execution is authorized.

## Architecture: Installed Workflows and Local Extensions

The installed `template` executable is the sole standard command surface. Root `justfile` recipes remain the stable repository-facing index and dispatch standard commands directly to `template`. The consumer-compiled local `stask` exists only for guarded repository-specific commands beneath `just x <name>`.

Reusable behavior belongs to the crate that owns its domain:

- `template-core` owns generic command, process, filesystem, repository-path, Git, TOML, output, temporary-workspace, hook, and runner capabilities.
- `template-schema` owns versioned declarations and lossless parsing for `template.config.toml`.
- `template-schema-engine` owns interpretation, validation, compatibility, planning, migration, and artifact reconciliation.
- `agentic-plugin` owns marketplace JSON and discovery-link mechanics; `template-docs-engine` owns Markdown discovery, migration, rendering, and generation.
- `template-cargo` owns ordinary Rust/Cargo developer workflows against already-converged files; `template-repo-analyzer` owns read-only facts and reports.
- `template-update` owns update phase ordering and failure propagation; `template-cli` owns installed parsing, standard composition, and user-facing reporting.
- `template-stask` owns only controlled registration and guarded execution of repository-specific `x` extensions.
- `rust-template` owns concrete Rust template policy and recipes. `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/**` owns reusable Rust guidance content (for the standard source, `agents-md-rs/fragments/**`), while `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**` owns only that repository's maintainer overlays.

Never put reusable workflow logic in a consumer `justfile`, shell script, or local `stask`. Add reusable behavior to its owner, expose complete standard behavior through `template-cli`, and keep project-only automation behind `x`.

Treat disconnected modules and command groups as architectural findings, then resolve them completely: reconnect live behavior through the correct façade or remove proven obsolete residue together with its tests, docs, errors, and dependencies. Do not add compatibility wiring or keep ghost APIs merely to silence diagnostics.

## Canonical Workflows

Use `just` as the repository-facing command index. Standard recipes invoke the installed `template` binary; only `just x <name>` enters the guarded local extension runner. Keep recipes, shell snippets, and CI YAML thin.

- Run `just repo-overview md` or `just repo-overview json` for live command ownership, gates, workspace layout, and generated-document facts.
- `just gen-md` materializes the configured `[guidance.source]` branch, composes `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/**` with optional `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**`, validates and renders the complete plan, writes changed targets, and cleans the temporary source checkout.
- `just migrate-md [PATH]...` maps maintained Markdown into target-local fragment inputs. Repeat `--target-slot <TARGET>=<SLOT>` for explicit reusable-slot placement; imports otherwise use the dynamic target-local tail.
- `just agent gates --staged`, `just agent gates --worktree`, and `just agent staged-summary` render repository-native agent reports without moving mutation or policy logic into the CLI adapter.
- Use the repository's declared full gates before handoff. A scoped command is diagnostic evidence, not a replacement for the required full-workspace gate.

### Template update contract

`just update-template [SOURCE] [--branch BRANCH]` reconciles a branch snapshot; it does not merge template history into the target.

- With no override, use the complete current `[template.source]`. A URL-only override retains the current branch, a branch-only override retains the current URL, and both arguments replace both fields.
- Validate schema compatibility, repository identity, normalized sources and paths, cross-section policy, and every static plan before target writes.
- Preserve target-owned source, layout, opt-outs, deviations, inactive ecosystems, comments, and unrelated formatting during template-owned adoption.
- Refresh dependencies only when managed declarations changed, then apply post-refresh dynamic reconciliation before managed children, plugins, and guidance.
- Persist the selected `[template.source]` only after reconciliation, cleanup, and guidance generation succeed. Earlier failure leaves the previous source authoritative.
- Legacy `[workspace.metadata.config]` and `rust-template.url` are bounded migration inputs only. Remove them after semantic equivalence and complete workflow success; never create a replacement source authority.
- Keep individual writes atomic and reruns convergent. Cleanup runs for every allocated workspace, and a primary failure plus cleanup failure must preserve both sources.

### Managed and generated surfaces

- Template-managed contracts are ownership rules. Use declared target entries, overrides, opt-outs, and deviations instead of fighting reconciled files.
- Marketplace and discovery-link reconciliation validates the full plan before writing, preserves unrelated entries and unknown JSON fields, rejects unsafe or occupied paths, and converges to a no-op on repeat.
- `[guidance.source]` is branch-tracked template-owned policy; `[guidance].regenerate` is the target-owned operational preference. Resolved commits are outcomes, never persisted authority.
- Target-local guidance overlays live only under `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**`; reusable guidance belongs only under `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/**`.

### Gate selection

- **Normal code change:** run `just fmt`, `just lint`, and `just test-all` before declaring the work complete.
- **Broader workflow/tooling change:** prefer `just ci`, which exercises the repository's configured formatting, lint, docs, test, coverage, supply-chain, duplication, and dead-code gates in CI order.
- **Coverage-sensitive change:** use the real coverage workflows and inspect touched-file results; never create filler branches, static exclusions, or tests that only move a percentage.
- **Feature-matrix change:** run `just hack` when behavior can differ across feature combinations.
- **Mutation-sensitive change:** run mutation workflows only when explicitly authorized, and keep cfg-aware applicability consistent between local and fleet execution.

### Scoped commands and hook behavior

`fmt`, `check`, `lint`, `test`, `test-doc`, `test-all`, and `doc` accept an optional leading path and a `--` passthrough. Root recipes forward `--from "{{invocation_directory()}}"` so scope resolution remains relative to the caller.

- `just lint` checks the full workspace; `just lint src` checks the crate owning `src`; `just lint -- --fix` forwards `--fix` to the underlying Cargo tool.
- `just cq` runs the configured complexity and duplication gates. Fix structural duplication or tune the owning algorithm; do not add static ignore files to hide reset residue.
- `just init` installs the generic launcher for `template precommit`. The launcher must fail clearly when `template` is unavailable and must never fall back to a local build or legacy `stask`.

## Implementation Constraints

- Follow the workspace formatter and lint policy exactly.
- Prefer descriptive snake_case for modules, files, and functions; use CamelCase for types and traits; use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants.
- Markdown prose and bullets stay unwrapped; do not hard-wrap `.md` documentation.

### Lint policy is absolute

**The workspace lint policies are not adjustable.** When a deny-level lint fires never silence at the call site, never propose downgrading the lint, never relax `Cargo.toml`/`clippy.toml`. If the clean fix is substantially larger than the immediate task, surface that to the user with a concrete proposal; do not paper over it with a shim.

### Look one layer upstream

Diagnostics are symptoms, not architecture. Before fixing a compile warning, Clippy warning, mutation survivor, coverage gap, generated-code lint, or test-fixture lint locally, identify the upstream owner of the shape: generator, macro expansion, parser model, API boundary, feature split, build workflow, or test harness.

- Do not rationalize new `#[allow]` / `#[expect]`, lint-policy changes, static exclusions, generated-output edits, compatibility shims, or non-idiomatic test fixtures because the current stage or command is narrower, the allowance was pre-existing, or the problematic code is generated.
- Code written during any stage must already align with the stricter end-state. If generated code or macro output triggers a lint, refactor the generator or expansion strategy so the generated code is clean.
- When tests need unusual macro or parser input, feed that input as parser data, expansion snapshots, typed compile diagnostics over generated temporary crates, or another non-production harness boundary instead of leaving non-idiomatic compiled tests that require allowances.
- Do not use "input data" or "compile-fail fixture" as an escape hatch. Negative compiler behavior is a valid behavior to test, but checked-in compile-failing Rust source is suspected architectural debt until proven otherwise. Keep a compile-diagnostic `.rs` fixture only when full `rustc` integration is the behavior under test, and normalize or delete incidental non-idiomatic syntax inside those fixtures.
- Preferred loop: identify the upstream owner, refactor there, add positive and negative behavior tests or expansion/workflow snapshots that pin the real contract, then remove the local lint debt.

Common things that fail to compile here but compile elsewhere:

- **`#[allow(...)]` / `#[expect(...)]`** — forbidden in sources, with one narrow exception: `#[allow(clippy::single_call_fn, reason = "...")]` is permitted where a named helper genuinely improves structure; a semantically and contextually relevant reason must be included. Fix the underlying issue rather than reaching for the exception if the named helper does not improve clarity & structure.
- **Panic-free everywhere — no test / debug / "production" carve-out.** Every runtime panic vector is forbidden in all code, tests included.
- **No `as` casts** — `as_conversions = "deny"`. Use `From` / `TryFrom` / `u64::try_from(...)`.
- **No raw arithmetic that may overflow** — `arithmetic_side_effects = "deny"` blocks `+` / `-` / `*` on integers. Use `checked_add` / `saturating_sub` / `wrapping_mul` and choose the operation that matches the domain semantics.
- **No `Box<dyn Trait>` / `&dyn Trait`** in most positions — static dispatch via generics / `impl Trait` is preferred (`borrowed_box`, `vec_box`, `redundant_allocation`, etc.).
- **No `async_trait`** — stdlib async-in-trait is stable since 2024 edition.
- **Disallowed identifiers / names / methods / types** are specified in `clippy.toml`.
- **Mod files:** `mod_module_files = "deny"` — use `foo.rs`, not `foo/mod.rs`.
- **Doc requirements:** `missing_docs = "deny"` for every `pub` item, and `missing_docs_in_private_items = "deny"` so private items carry doc comments too; `missing_errors_doc` / `missing_panics_doc` / `missing_safety_doc` for fns. Every fallible `pub fn` needs a `# Errors` section.

### Error model

- Use typed errors via `thiserror`.
- Wrapping third-party errors is fine when the dependency's own error is a real typed error. Reusable crates should keep their own error enums; local `stask` code should map those errors at the adapter boundary so command behavior and diagnostics stay stable.

## Testing Contract

- Keep unit tests adjacent to the code they cover with `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`.
- Use clear test names such as `detects_overflow` or `adds_small_values`.
- Put executable examples in public API docs so `just test-doc` exercises them.
- **Tests are panic-free** (assertion macros, `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!`, `proptest!` / `prop_assert*` / `prop_assume!`, etc., are all banned). Signal failure by returning `Result<(), TestFailure>` through the `ensure*` helpers from `strict-test-support`.
- **Property tests** declare the strict `proptest` fork directly: build strategies and combinators through `proptest`, then execute them through `proptest::strict::ensure_property`. The property closure returns `Result<(), TestFailure>` and uses the generic `strict_test_support::ensure*` assertions like any test body. The strict runner is deterministically seeded; `just fuzz` reruns the suite with a random seed for an exploratory entropy run.
- **Snapshot tests** temporarily go through `strict_test_support::ensure_snapshot` (`snapbox`'s Result-based `Assert::try_eq` behind the vocabulary), comparing rendered text against committed `tests/snapshots/<name>.snap` files. Refresh stale snapshots with `just snap-update` and review the rewritten files with `git diff`.
- **Compile-diagnostics tests** declare the strict `trybuild` fork directly: create one mutable `trybuild::TestCases`, register both `pass` and `compile_fail` cases, and return its explicit typed `run()` result. Compare compile-fail fixtures against adjacent `.stderr` snapshots and require pass fixtures to compile and run cleanly. Refresh compiler diagnostics with `TRYBUILD=overwrite` and review the rewritten `.stderr` files with `git diff`; keep this signal separate from `SNAPSHOTS` because diagnostics churn with toolchain releases.

### Coverage and test quality

Coverage is a backstop; meaningful behavior tests are the obligation. Every file you create or touch is in scope, including pre-existing gaps in that file. Write positive and negative coverage for every behavior first, then use coverage output to find missed paths.

The numeric target is above 90% on every coverage measure — the `regions`, `functions`, `lines`, and (when the active mode measures them) `branches` columns `just coverage` reports. The workspace `TOTAL` row must clear 90% on every measured column. `just coverage --per-file` also enforces per-file backstops; `just ci` runs both the normal per-file coverage gate and the per-feature union coverage gate where the template exposes them. Those per-file floors are deliberately below the 90% target at demonstrated-achievable thresholds for irreducible artifact gaps, but the design target remains 90%+ for every file.

- **The percentage never justifies these — each one outranks a higher number.** While pushing coverage up you may not:
  - invent test-only machinery (classifier enums, comparison wrappers, discriminant helpers) whose only purpose is to dodge a `matches!` / `if let` dead arm;
  - reformat code solely to move llvm-cov's line attribution (e.g. collapsing a multi-line `ensure(\n …,\n)?` onto one line just to relocate the `?` region);
  - add an assertion that asserts nothing meaningful, or pin an incidental implementation detail, to move the number;
  - delete or weaken a meaningful test to lift a file's percentage;
  - drop or weaken a typed error, a portability guard/skip, or an idiomatic panic-free assertion (`matches!` on a non-`PartialEq` typed error or `bpaf::ParseFailure`, or an exhaustive match forced by the no-`_` `wildcard_enum_match_arm` rule) to make a branch reachable;
  - relax the lint policy, the `dupes.toml` thresholds, or add an `#[allow]`-based coverage exclusion.

Some gaps are irreducible without one of the above: `matches!` / `if let` on non-`PartialEq` types leaves a never-taken arm; code that spawns or `execv`s (the coverage runner spawning `llvm-cov`, the pre-commit-hook bin's `main` + re-exec, the core precommit handoff) cannot instrument itself; deliberate git-availability portability skips leave a dead branch. When a file's only remaining gap is one of these, leave it at the per-file floor and stop — that is exactly what the lower per-file floor exists for. Reach for the clean levers first: exact-value comparisons (`==` on tuples / arrays / `Vec`s, or deriving `PartialEq` on a comparable type) instead of an always-true `matches!`; a tail `ensure(...)` instead of a redundant `ensure(...)?; Ok(())`; extracting a pure decision from an I/O wrapper and testing it directly (the `duplication::classify_exit` / `cyclomatic::evaluate` pattern).
- **Both polarities, every live behavior.** Every supported behavior gets a positive *and* a negative test: what does happen (this input yields this result, this branch is taken, this `Ok` is returned) and what does not (this invalid input is rejected, this guard fires, this `Err` variant is returned). Negative tests are for still-supported behavior, invalid inputs, compatibility contracts, safety boundaries, and regression-prone invariants. They are not a license to preserve tests for deleted features.
- **Mutation applicability is behavior.** When mutation tooling filters cfg-inactive source, build feature matrices, or forwards work into distributed/fleet runners, tests must cover both included and excluded paths using real command/config inputs. Assert that active, unknown, or any-target-active cfg contexts stay in scope, and that source is excluded only when manifest declarations, Cargo config, env rustflags, and target cfg facts make it provably inactive for the run.
- **Do not test ghosts.** When removing any capability or behavior, delete its behavior tests and documentation with it. This applies across product APIs, workflow surfaces, file formats, generated artifacts, dependencies, integrations, commands, flags, and pipelines. Do not add assertions that a removed thing is absent or that a deleted path does not run unless that absence is itself a live user-facing contract, and name that contract in the test. A test that exists only to prove a non-existent thing remains non-existent is fake rigor.
- **No coverage-gaming, no filler.** Each test asserts a real, observable behavioral contract. A test that exercises code only to move the number, asserts nothing meaningful, or pins an incidental implementation detail is worse than no test — it locks in noise and has to be rewritten later. Write the test the behavior deserves and let coverage follow.

## Generated Artifacts and Hooks

Run the repository's real workflows and report their fallout. Do not substitute weaker check-only commands or redesign around a dirty worktree.

- `just gen-md` resolves the configured guidance branch, reads reusable content from `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/**`, combines it with `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**`, renders every target before writing, updates only changed files, and reconciles each generated `AGENTS.md` companion as exact `@./AGENTS.md` content.
- Edit reusable guidance only in `<guidance-source-repo>/<fragments-root>/**` (for the standard source, `agents-md-rs/fragments/**`); edit repository-specific maintainer guidance only in `<consumer-repo>/docs/fragments/**`. Never move local names or policies into the reusable package.
- `just gen-lint-template` rewrites generated lint references from the live toolchain.
- Coverage and code-quality workflows may refresh ignored reports under `cov/`; badge and pre-commit workflows may refresh committed files under `badges/`. Treat `cov/` as transient diagnostics, never stage it, and regenerate the complete badge set instead of selectively patching SVGs.
- `just snap-update` may rewrite committed snapshots; compiler-diagnostic overwrite modes may rewrite adjacent diagnostic snapshots. Review generated changes as workflow output.
- The pre-commit workflow runs CI, the documentation supplement, and badges/metrics before staging the union of changed artifacts exactly once.
- Preserve unrelated user changes and report command fallout plainly; never hand-edit generated outputs to suppress diagnostics or retain obsolete product names.

## Commit & Pull Request Guidelines

- **Subject:** `type(scope): structural imperative description/summary`. `type` is one of `feat` / `fix` / `refactor` / `docs` / `test` / `build` / `ci` / `perf` / `style`; `scope` is required. **`chore` is never valid** — pick the precise type (dep bump → `build`, CI tweak → `ci`, doc edit → `docs`, formatting-only → `style`).
- **Body:** 1 to 5 sections. Each section starts with a plain-text heading line (no `#` markers, no trailing colon, no underline) immediately followed by 3 to 5 bullet list items (no blank line between heading and bullets). Sections are separated from each other by exactly one blank line. No prose paragraphs — bullets only. Do not pad to multiple sections artificially; one section is fine for small changes.
- **PRs** should explain the change, note affected crates or tooling, link related issues when relevant, and list the commands you ran (typically `just ci`). Update `README.md` or automation docs when workflow or policy changes.
- **Commit framing:** foreground the repository's product/API behavior when a staged change mixes product changes with template-update fallout. Treat `stask/`, coverage, badges, mutation, duplication, and workflow artifacts as supporting context unless the commit's primary purpose is genuinely template automation.
